title: How to be happy

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Positive psychology expert Sheila Panchal, founder of Happiness First, who works with organizations and individuals, explains: 'Psychologists have identified three elements to happiness – having pleasures in life, being engaged by using your strengths on a regular basis, and experiencing a sense of meaning by feeling part of something greater than yourself.' For instance, when you are absorbed in a conversation, work or a hobby you may have an experience known as flow where you won't feel joy or pleasure at the time, but afterwards you have a deep sense of satisfaction that you may reflect on for a considerable time. Flow is a particularly vital aspect of future happiness. According to the US General Social Survey, happiness is derived from, in order of importance: family relationships, finances, work, well-developed social networks and health.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Those who are happy with their lives have stronger immune systems when exposed to the flu virus, they are more able to resist it-and they recover from surgery faster. They also tend to live longer. That's the conclusion from an analysis of autobiographical essays by new nuns entering an American convent from 1932. Psychologists rated these essays for positive feelings expressed and found a correlation with how long each nun lived. Put simply, twice as many of the unhappier nuns died earlier compared to their happier colleagues.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The relationship between money and happiness is complex. 'If you're below the breadline, then extra money makes a difference to your happiness but after a certain point, extra money does not make you that much happier,' says Panchal. In Britain, the United States and Japan, although wages have more than doubled over the last fifty years, this does not appear to have contributed to an increase in human happiness according to long-running surveys. Why? One answer is that we start to compare ourselves with others and this creates discontent. In a recent study, Harvard University students were asked what they would prefer – a world where they got $50,000 a year and everyone else got $25,000, or one where their earnings were doubled to $100,000, but others got more – a quarter of a million dollars. The majority preferred the first world where they got less in absolute terms, but at least it was more than everyone else. If you must compare, do it downwards. That's why Olympic bronze medallists are happier about their efforts than silver medallists – the former are grateful they've got something, the latter are anguished by the fact they missed out on the gold.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Studies on twins show a strong genetic component in happiness and depression. This not just because twins share the same surroundings – research on identical twins brought up apart shows the same result. However, the genes involved in happiness are unknown and, as with all psychological attributes, it is likely that many different genes are responsible. Drugs can boost serotonin levels and so lift depression and improve mood. But even if you are born miserable, you can still learn to be happier by changing your outlook and attitude. As far as brain science is concerned, Dr Richard Davidson of the University of Wisconsin has shown that positive feelings are linked to more electrical activity on the left frontal lobe of the brain, and negative feelings to the right frontal lobe. Happy people, those who report positive feelings and who smile more, exhibit more of this left brain activity.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Happiness around the world is tracked by projects such as the World Database of Happiness, which has found that the populations in Western countries, such as Britain have not got any happier since 1950, despite massive increases in our levels of comfort. Dr Richard Stevens, formerly Head of Psychology at the Open University in the UK, identifies two major barriers to achieving happiness in the 21st century: the car and the media. Cars isolate you from the local community so that your neighborhood and town centre more often feel like threatening places rather than a positive resource. Television (and to a lesser extent, print media)exposes people to violence, bad news and consumer pressures, which create fear and discontent. TV watching is also passive and takes away time that could be used for much more satisfying 'flow' activities.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: On the basis of his long-standing research, Dr Stevens claims happiness comes from the body, relationships, and learning to direct your thoughts in a positive way. Dr Stevens says that in order to sustain a level of happiness you should: 'Take exercise and watch your diet, work at caring, loving relationships with family and a small group of others, give these relationships the time they need. Smile at strangers and colleagues, make small gestures and, above all, list the good things you have to be grateful for.'
